chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Learning to read and arrange: Lloyd Hunter, Nat Towles and Jim Bell's
summary: Challenged, he studied reading and writing, moved to Lloyd Hunter and then Nat Towles, played Jim Bell's club in Omaha, and became a good arranger largely self-taught.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yes, I am. Yes, I am. Well, in staying with that band you began to be able to cope with reading the music, for instance, or your reading was improving that much, was it? Or had it already improved that much?

Yes. I had been challenged and I had been encouraged to study more. Now, this all comes slowly and it came slowly. And I'm still studying music as most musicians do. So in my desire to better myself I realized that I had to study, so in the process I started to studying music more seriously, and learning to read better, and also learning to write. And it was during this time that I left this first band that I played with, because they weren't working regularly enough and I had learned from the experience in St. Louis that I had to make money as well as enjoy, so I joined a more successful band known as Lloyd Hunter.
Yes, I see. How long did you stay with Lloyd Hunter?
I stayed with Lloyd Hunter for several months and then I joined another band which was a better band, by the name of Nat Towles.

And it was in these bands, after I had played for a short time in a night club in Omaha, Nebraska called Jim Bells that I had learned to write music rather well, and I was considered to be one of the good jazz arrangers in that area.
That was very quickly done from over a period of what, about 18 months. All that.
Right, right, right. In that period I learned to write music.
Did you -- were you self taught, learning to write music?

More or less, more or less. As I said my knowledge of studying music in school, I had the fundamental basics, and I learned from other musicians. I had little sessions, you know, we got together, people were friendly, and musicians exchanged ideas. And I studied arranging on my own. I got the books and I read them, and you know, you go to the library and you pick up a few books here and there, and you talk to a few experts. And I also had the feeling of
jazz, which was important in writing this music, you see.
